Address all modifiable cardiovascular risk factors, initiate cascade screening, and start high-intensity statin therapy and aspirin, 81 mg, daily Lp(a) is proatherogenic, prothrombotic, and proinflammatory1,2and has an estimated global prevalence of around 20%.1While the upper Lp(a) threshold that indicates an elevated ASCVD risk does vary, values above the 80th (100 nmol/L) or 85th (125 nmol/L) are clinically accepted.1,3Although Lp(a)-lowering therapies are currently under investigation, elevated Lp(a) is actionable. This patient’s elevated Lp(a) level is concerning due to his FHx of premature ASCVD and South Asian ancestry. Despite being at low 10-year ASCVD risk by the PCEs, he was noted to have 3 risk-enhancing factors (REFs). The presence of 3 or more REFs may incrementally increase ASCVD risk beyond the PCE estimates.4In individuals with a FHx of premature ASCVD, risk stratification using the PCEs may not be high enough to merit consideration and points to a unique use of the REFs. This patient’s clinical management can be improved by (1) counseling, (2) coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring to guide medical therapy, and (3) cascade screening of family members. Counseling patients about the association between elevated Lp(a) and ASCVD should underscore the need for comprehensively treating all modifiable ASCVD risk factors. While treating risk factors does not lower Lp(a) levels, it can reduce overall ASCVD risk. Lifestyle modifications outlined in the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 can significantly reduce ASCVD risk.1,2CAC scoring is recommended when a risk decision for statin therapy is uncertain. Indeed, with this patient’s FHx and elevated Lp(a) level, risk information to support statin therapy is already available. However, a significantly elevated CAC score could support more intensive lipid-lowering and aspirin therapy. A CAC score and Lp(a) level add independently to risk stratification in these individuals.1,2While PCSK9 inhibitors can lower Lp(a) by 15% to 25%, therapy should focus on lowering low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), which has greater ASCVD risk reduction per mmol/L.1,2Given that approximately 80% to 90% of an individual’s Lp(a) level is genetically determined in an autosomal codominant inheritance pattern,1cascade screening, a high-yield method of screening first-degree relatives who have a much higher likelihood of having the abnormal trait, may be warranted (Figure 2). Given the elevated CAC score (137 Agatston units) and percentile (94th), this patient started high-intensity statin therapy and 81 mg of aspirin daily.2,5Cascade screening was offered to this patient’s first- and second-degree family members. This case highlights the complexities in the management of individuals with elevated Lp(a) who, owing to their young age, may have a low 10-year ASCVD risk calculated by PCEs. The 2018 cholesterol guidelines3called out individuals with likely familial hypercholesterolemia who have an LDL-C level of 160 to 89 mg/dL and a FHx of premature ASCVD. A similar rationale would apply in this patient with a high-risk ethnic background with strikingly elevated Lp(a) level and a FHx of premature ASCVD. Although this should be addressed by future guidelines, we believe that together these high-risk, long-term personal traits merit an intensive LDL-C and apolipoprotein B–lowering regimen.

scenario: A man in his mid-50s with a history of mitral valve repair presented to the emergency department with complaints of recent-onset palpitation within the last hour. On physical examination, the patient showed a rhythmic tachycardia with a rate of 178 beats/min and blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg. The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a regular tachycardia with a rate of 178 beats/min; no obvious P waves were recognizable (Figure 1A). The QRS complexes displayed 2 different morphologies occurring with a definite allorhythmic distribution: pairs of beats exhibiting complete right bundle branch block (RBBB) and QRS duration of 140 milliseconds followed by a third beat with normal configuration and QRS duration of 70 milliseconds. This trigeminal variation in intraventricular conduction occurred without any change in cycle length and was maintained. Adenosine administration quickly slowed the ventricular rate allowing recognition of an atrial tachycardia with a rate of 178/min and a 2:1 atrioventricular (AV) ratio (Figure 1B).

explanation: Atypical atrial flutter with RBBB aberration and conduction improvement every third beat resulting from concealed type I (Wenckebach) second-degree block in the right bundle branch with 3:2 ratio C. Start treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin and amiodarone The atrial rate during adenosine administration was identical to the ventricular rate during tachycardia, implying that the arrhythmia inFigure 1A reflects an atrial tachycardia with 1:1 AV conduction. The medical history strongly suggests a macroreentrant circuit (macroreentrant atrial tachycardia, also calledatypical atrial flutter) developing around the atriotomy scar related to mitral valve surgery, possibly a left-sided atrial flutter such as mitral annular flutter. The R-R interval prolongation due to the shift from 1:1 to 2:1 AV ratio restored the normal right bundle branch conduction resulting in narrow QRS complexes. This supports an intermittent phase 3 RBBB. The most challenging issue in the tracing on presentation is the periodic disappearance of the RBBB aberration. The key to the correct diagnosis is the unexpected normalization of the QRS morphology occurring periodically, every third beat, despite constant cycle lengths.1-4 A pattern of complete bundle branch block does not necessarily imply a total interruption of conduction in the affected bundle branch but can also result from a delay exceeding the time required for activation from the contralateral bundle branch (accepted critical delay: 40-60 milliseconds).3In a Wenckebach series, whenever the opening beat is normally conducted whereas complete bundle branch block occurs in the second impulse, progressive conduction delays in later beats and final failure do not further affect QRS morphology and width: the bundle branch Wenckebach phenomenon, therefore, is “incompletely concealed” being inapparent on ECG only from the second to the closing beat of each sequence.3,4As illustrated schematically inFigure 2, while the conduction through the left bundle branch is normal, the right bundle branch shows increasingly impaired conduction owing to an area of refractoriness leading to progressive prolongation of the conduction time, until a block occurs in the third impulse of each Wenckebach series. Impulse 1 conducts down both bundle branches normally (conduction time: 40 milliseconds), resulting in narrow QRS. Impulse 2 penetrates the critical area within the right bundle branch with delayed conduction (right bundle conduction time: 90 milliseconds). Although a complete block in the right bundle branch does not occur, the delayed conduction results in ventricular depolarization via the left bundle branch, resulting in a complete RBBB pattern. Impulse 3 represents further impaired conduction and a true block in the right bundle branch. The proximal bidirectional block during the third impulse of each Wenckebach sequence doubles the effective cycle length of the right bundle branch, increasing its recovery time to 2 R-R intervals, thereby allowing normal conduction of impulse 4. This prolonged cycle length, furthermore, extends the right bundle refractory period following the normalized beat so that the second impulse of the next Wenckebach sequence once again conducts with RBBB aberration, and the mechanism then repeats.1,2Accordingly, the Wenckebach phenomenon in the right bundle branch is incompletely concealed and is evident only on the first to second beats.3,4Incompletely concealed Wenckebach-type block in a bundle branch was first postulated by Rosenbaum in 1969 in order to explain periodical improvements of aberrant conduction unrelated to changes in cycle length.3 Alternate explanations are less convincing. Disappearance of the RBBB pattern every third beat theoretically could reflect fusion of supraventricular impulses with trigeminal right ventricular extrasystoles. However, a regular repetition of such ectopics in a fixed trigeminal rhythm with perfect synchronization with atrial impulses is unlikely; furthermore, no ventricular extrasystoles were evidenced throughout the tracing.1,2The findings in this ECG are compatible with a 3:1 RBBB. However, such a high conduction ratio in a bundle branch is extremely rare especially in a repetitive fashion. Moreover, in order to invoke a 3:1 RBBB, a very long right bundle branch refractory period, extending over 2 cardiac cycles (>675 milliseconds), has to be assumed. Nevertheless, as the rate slows with adenosine and normal right bundle conduction resumes, some R-R intervals measuring 630 to 670 milliseconds occur (Figure 1B), which excludes this possibility.3,4 Although the conduction disturbance may have been the result of mitral valve surgery, a Wenckebach-type bundle branch block occurring at fast rates does not necessarily indicate a damaged conduction system, but may represent merely a functional, phase 3 delay in the distal His-Purkinje system.1Amiodarone infusion restored sinus rhythm, leading to persistent normalization of intraventricular conduction. Given the very recent onset of tachycardia and the low risk of stroke, postcardioversion anticoagulation was omitted.5,6No recurrence of atrial flutter and/or RBBB was documented over a 1-year follow-up while receiving oral amiodarone.

scenario: A man in his early 20s presented with suspected syncope and shaking with no significant medical history. The patient fell asleep and his girlfriend tried to wake him, but he started shaking and slumped over on the ground. He denied confusion afterward but did not feel well with nausea, flushing, chest tightness, and a rapid heart rate. explanation: Brugada type 1 syndrome with unexplained syncope The key to the correct diagnosis in this case was the ECG that was consistent with spontaneous Brugada type 1 morphology with more than 2-mm coved ST-segment elevation in leads V1 and V2 (Figure). Recognition of the Brugada type 1 pattern as a potential cause of cardio-arrhythmogenic syncope is important. The incidence of the Brugada type 1 ECG pattern in the US is thought to be as low as 0.03%.1The proposed Shanghai Score System2can be used for the diagnosis of Brugada syndrome, which relies on ECG, clinical history, family history, or genetic test results. A score of more than 3.5 points is thought to be probable and/or definite Brugada. Brugada type 1 can present asymptomatically, in which case the management is observation. However, in those with symptomatic features, such as unexplained cardiac arrest or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation arrest, nocturnal agonal respirations, atrial fibrillation/flutter in patients younger than 30 years of age, or syncope of uncertain etiology, further evaluation is needed. In patients with unexplained syncope in the setting of Brugada syndrome, ventricular fibrillation should be strongly considered. The presence of suspected arrhythmogenic syncope alone in patients with Brugada syndrome with the spontaneous type 1 electrocardiogram pattern is a class 1 indication for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD).3An electrophysiology study for risk stratification prior to ICD placement, however, is a class 2B recommendation and is controversial. For those with symptomatic refractory Brugada syndrome or repeated ICD shocks, there is a role for epicardial ablation. During our initial evaluation, we felt seizures were lower in the differential diagnosis, however, a striking feature was his persistent muscle jerks, making convulsive syncope less likely. We felt the margin of error was quite small and the patient ultimately decided to undergo transvenous ICD placement. The decision to offer an ICD is not one to take lightly. The incidence of at least 1 inappropriate ICD shock from an ICD has been reported as high as 6.6% during a median follow-up of 2 years.4There is also the obstacle of generator changes in a young patient, which can be necessary anywhere from 5 to 10 years depending on the manufacturer used. There is also the decision of whether or not to pursue a subcutaneous ICD system when there is no indication for pacing, which has largely been shown to be noninferior to the transvenous system,5and this choice is largely driven by patient preference. As such, it is very prudent to have a systematic approach, which is largely guideline driven when offering ICDs to patients, and this played a large role in our decision to pursue such an extensive medical workup to validate the uncertain etiology of our patient’s syncope. The patient received a 7-day postdevice follow-up examination.  He was mending well and able to resume regular activities.

Recognition of the pVAD as a potential cause of iatrogenic MR is important, as acute severe MR requires prompt early surgical intervention. Frequent complications after pVAD placement include thrombus formation, tamponade, right ventricular failure, and hypovolemia. To our knowledge, there have been very few case reports of iatrogenic MR in patients with pVAD.1,2Possible mechanisms of injury are damage to the mitral valve apparatus during the insertion of pVAD or subsequent migration of the device. In fulminant myocarditis, it is hypothesized that the myocardial tissue is inflamed and friable, making it more susceptible to injury.3In this patient, the pVAD was placed emergently when the patient was hemodynamically unstable. While receiving ECMO support, the complete hemodynamic effect of MR is usually not apparent owing to the altered physiology. Severe MR and flail leaflet were only apparent after ECMO decannulation. Acute severe MR is not well tolerated and typically is a surgical emergency. Early surgical intervention compared with watchful waiting is associated with improved survival.4The American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association guidelines for the management of patients with primary MR indicate intraoperative transesophageal echocardiogram to establish the mechanism, and mitral repair is recommended, if possible, rather than mitral valve replacement.5In some cases, rapid decompensation may preclude meaningful surgical options. Additionally, mitral valve repair may not always be feasible depending on the extent of damage to the mitral apparatus. Sef and colleagues6reported 4 patients with mitral valve damage associated with pVAD. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair was performed in 1 patient for severe MR.7In 2 patients, valve replacement was required owing to the extent of valvular injury,2,8and in 1 patient, surgery was not possible.1In this patient, the mitral valve was repaired successfully in the setting of fulminant myocarditis, thus preventing the need for lifelong anticoagulation related to a mechanical prosthesis in a young woman of childbearing potential. There are alternative left ventricular venting options for peripheral ECMO, including intra-aortic balloon pump and left atrial-to-femoral artery bypass (TandemHeart, CardiacAssist). Left atrial decompression with percutaneous transseptal puncture and insertion of left atrial drain, transseptal balloon and blade septostomy, and percutaneous insertion of a pulmonary artery or retrograde transaortic catheter can also be considered for venting in peripheral ECMO.9 At the 30-day postoperative follow-up visit, the patient was recuperating well and able to resume regular activities.

scenario: A man in his 40s was seen in clinic for a long history of palpitations. He had a history of cardiac arrest after receiving adenosine for sustained supraventricular tachycardia and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. The patient was also noted to have episodes of atrial flutter. Transthoracic echocardiogram displayed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 63% and mild aortic and mitral regurgitation. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging in sinus rhythm showed mild left ventricle thickening (up to 14 mm) and was otherwise normal. The patient was hospitalized for initiation of sotalol, given that he experienced frequent episodes of atrial arrhythmia.Figure 1A shows sinus rhythm prior to sotalol initiation.Figure 1B shows telemetry during administration of sotalol.
explanation: Latent accessory pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) B. Electrophysiology study and catheter ablation Prior to sotalol loading, the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) (Figure1A) showed sinus rhythm at 57 beats per minute with a normal axis and QT interval. There were no Q waves in the lateral leads. There were inferolateral precordial T-wave abnormalities. With sotalol loading, the telemetry strip (Figure1B) revealed widening of the QRS complex. The differential diagnosis included (1) rate-related aberrancy, (2) idioventricular rhythm, (3) phase 4 aberrancy, and (4) preexcitation from an atrioventricular pathway. Phase 3 or 4 aberrancy was unlikely because the sinus rate had not changed significantly. An idioventricular rhythm resulting in this finding would have to be perfectly isorhythmic to maintain constant PR intervals. The short, fixed PR interval with wide QRS complex makes ventricular preexcitation from an atrioventricular pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) the most likely diagnosis.1Electrophysiology study and catheter ablation provide high likelihood of cure. Amiodarone is not indicated in a young patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome; ST segment changes are due to altered ventricular repolarization owing to preexcitation rather than ischemia. Exercise treadmill testing is not useful with lack of ischemia or exposure to medications with use dependence (class I). The ECG initially did not show clear ventricular preexcitation. An accessory pathway that is not capable of antegrade conduction will not be apparent on an ECG in sinus rhythm; this is termedconcealed preexcitation.2However, with sotalol loading, anterograde conduction with delta waves develops in this patient without a change in heart rate. Absent delta waves in the presence of an accessory pathway capable of anterograde conduction has been termedlatent preexcitation.3The proposed mechanism for this phenomenon is due to relative conduction times from the sinus node through the atrioventricular node vs across the atrium and the accessory pathway. Conditions that may cause latent preexcitation include left-lateral pathways, delay in intra-atrial conduction time, or increased left-atrial size. Some evidence exists that this phenomenon may occur when autonomic influences on the pathway and on atrioventricular nodal conduction are opposite.4Additionally, concealed retrograde conduction into the accessory pathway during sinus rhythm could prevent preexcitation and eliminate delta waves. Sotalol has been studied for treatment of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia  in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome but has not been reported to reveal a latent accessory pathway. Sotalol causes an increase in the retrograde effective refractory period of accessory pathways, whereas changes in the anterograde refractory periods were more variable.5,6It is unlikely that sotalol improved conduction in the accessory pathway. Instead, sotalol slows atrioventricular nodal conduction and may prevent concealed retrograde conduction into the pathway in a manner analogous to transseptal concealed conduction for perpetuation of bundle-branch block. Repeated 12-lead ECG confirmed manifest preexcitation (short PR intervals and delta waves,Figure 2). Negative delta waves in leads II, III, and aVF and QRS transition between V1and V2argues for a posteroseptal pathway.7The patient then developed a narrow-complex short RP tachycardia showing negative P waves in the inferior leads consistent with a posterior accessory pathway-mediated orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia. The tachycardia was terminated with the Valsalva maneuver. After providing consent, the patient underwent successful catheter ablation of the posteroseptal pathway and cavotricuspid isthmus (for typical right-atrial flutter). The successful ablation site was the anterior floor of the coronary sinus body, about 1 to 2 cm from the coronary sinus ostium. Sotalol treatment was discontinued, and the patient was discharged with metoprolol and lisinopril therapy.

explanation: D. Sequencing of mitochondrial DNA In the present case, the constellation of short stature, sensorineural deafness, and mild cognitive impairment, in addition to significant cardiac hypertrophy, suggested the possibility of mitochondrial disease. Further investigation with sequencing of mitochondrial DNA from cutaneous fibroblasts revealed a 3243A>G point mitochondrial DNA mutation, confirming the diagnosis of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. The degree of heteroplasmy was subsequently determined with droplet digital polymerase chain reaction to quantify wild-type and m.3243A>G copy number.1The mitochondrial DNA mutation rate was as high as 90.8% in cardiomyocytes, compared with 29% in skin fibroblasts. Subsequently, endomyocardial biopsy was performed and revealed mitochondrial hyperplasia and morphological abnormalities of cristae (Figure). Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy is characterized by an oxidative phosphorylation disorder due to genetic mutations in genes encoding the structure and function of myocardial mitochondria. Mutations of both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA can cause mitochondrial cardiomyopathy, which is typically recognized as a generalized manifestation of neurological and metabolic disorders.2Cardiomyopathy, however, can be the only phenotype of mitochondrial disease and is often misdiagnosed.3Cardiac manifestations vary from asymptomatic to catastrophic heart failure or sudden death.4The frequency of cardiac involvement (ie, cardiomyopathy) in mitochondrial diseases is 20% to 40%5; hypertrophic remodeling, which can mimic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), is observed in approximately 40%, especially in mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) syndrome.6 Unlike patients who have classic MELAS with young-onset stroke-like episodes and encephalopathy characterized by seizures or dementia or both, this patient most strongly demonstrated the cardiac manifestation, which is most likely due to the significant elevation of the rate of heteroplasmy in cardiomyocytes to 90.8%. A positive correlation has been shown between the rate of mitochondrial DNA 3243A>G mutation and the degree of cardiac hypertrophy.7Therefore, the high rate of gene mutation in cardiomyocytes of the present patient might have contributed to the phenotype of HCM-like morphology in the heart. Furthermore, the patient did not have any signs or symptoms of heart failure (HF) when he was diagnosed with mitochondrial cardiomyopathy due to 3243A>G mitochondrial DNA mutation. Notwithstanding, previously reported cases of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy have had characteristics of partial mitochondrial disease, most of which presented with progressive shortness of breath due to worsening HF.8,9If the phenotype of mitochondrial disease is localized most significantly to the heart, the diagnosis of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy can easily be overlooked. Accordingly, considering the diagnosis of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy in the context of HCM-like hypertrophy would be important, especially in cases with concomitant symptoms. A standard treatment for mitochondrial cardiomyopathy has not been established. In general, the management of patients with mitochondrial cardiomyopathy should follow clinical practice guidelines for HF including an important role of medical and device therapies. Furthermore, current research strategies are dedicated toward improving mitochondrial function in patients with mitochondrial disorders.1 The patient has been well and without HF symptoms while undergoing guideline-directed medical therapy for HF including a β-blocker, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging The key to diagnosis here is a history of palpitations in a young otherwise healthy patient, T wave inversions in leads V1through V3, and severely dilated, dyskinetic right ventricle (RV) with trabeculations on echocardiogram. Timely recognition of this potentially fatal condition and further evaluation with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is important to avoid unnecessary workup including catheterization or computed tomographic angiography. With a prevalence of 1:5000, arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia/cardiomyopathy is a notable familial disorder that predominantly affects the RV and is one of the leading causes of arrhythmic cardiac arrest in young people and athletes.1,2Typically inherited as an autosomal dominant disease, the genes encoding desmosomal proteins play a key role in its pathogenesis.3 The distinctive histopathology of arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy is the loss of RV myocardium, with the substitution of fibrofatty tissue, which progresses from the epicardium toward the endocardium, resulting in wall thinning and aneurysmal dilatation, typically in the so-called triangle of dysplasia, ie, inflow tract (subtricuspid region), outflow tract (infundibular region), and apex.4 The most common clinical presentations are palpitations or effort-induced syncope in an adolescent or young adult, with T wave inversions in the right precordial leads (V1through V4), ventricular arrhythmias of a left bundle-branch block morphology with superior axis, and RV abnormalities on imaging.1,5Patients with longstanding disease may develop end-stage RV or biventricular pump failure.1 Diagnosis of arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia relies on combined assessment of structural, functional, and electrophysiologic abnormalities. Epsilon wave or inverted T waves in right precordial leads in individuals older than 14 years (in the absence of right bundle-branch block) are considered a major criterion. On imaging, major criteria include regional RV akinesia, dyskinesia, or aneurysm, with RV outflow tract end-diastolic dimension of 32 mm or more on parasternal long axis or 36 mm or more on parasternal short axis or fractional area change of 33% or less on 2-dimensional echocardiogram, and a ratio of RV end-diastolic volume to body surface area 110 mL/m2or more (male individuals) or RV ejection fraction of 40% or less on magnetic resonance imaging.6 Genetic testing is of limited value because disease-causing genes are identified in approximately 50% of patients who meet the revised Task Force Criteria,6and 16% of healthy individuals have missense variants in one of the major arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy susceptibility genes. A definitive diagnosis is based on histologic demonstration of fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium at biopsy, surgery, or autopsy.1 Patients are advised to abstain from intense physical activity. Despite insufficient evidence, β-blockers are recommended and amiodarone or sotalol is often added for synergistic effect to prevent arrhythmias. An implanted cardioverter-defibrillator is recommended for primary prevention. While cardiac transplantation is the ultimate therapy for patients with recurrent arrhythmias, catheter ablation is considered a palliative approach.1,7 The patient underwent a magnetic resonance imaging that showed markedly enlarged RV with end-diastolic volume index of 180 mL/m2, RV ejection fraction of 14%, extensive delayed enhancement, and marked trabeculation confirming the diagnosis of arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia (Figure 2). He started taking β-blockers and was referred for implanted cardioverter-defibrillator placement.

explanation: Biatrial intracardiac mass and multiple systemic lesions secondary to IgG4-related disease D. Perform an endomyocardial biopsy The patient underwent transcatheter endomyocardial biopsy, endobronchial ultrasonography-guided biopsy, and excisional biopsy of her nasal septal mass. The histology of the sampled tissues showed chronic inflammatory infiltrate with no evidence for malignancy. Immunohistochemistry analyses confirmed a large number of IgG4+ plasma cells. Based on the histology results, our final diagnosis was IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD). Her cardiac mass was considered inoperable given its complex anatomy and multichamber involvement. She initially received high-dose steroid therapy with prednisone over subsequent months with minimal radiological improvement. Rituximab was added as a second agent, which she received at 6-month intervals for a total duration of 24 months. This resulted in significant reduction in the size of the cardiac mass and right Meckel cave lesions, as demonstrated on her repeat cardiac and brain magnetic resonance imaging (Figure 2), suggestive of IgG4-RD. IgG4-RD is a fibroinflammatory disease associated with increased number of IgG4+ plasma cells within tissue and tendency to form tumorlike lesions at multiple sites. It is a relatively new disease entity and has only been recognized as a systemic condition in the past 20 years.1,2It was first described in the pancreas but has since been reported in nearly every organ system.3,4There is overlap in imaging findings with other inflammatory and neoplastic conditions; therefore, tissue biopsy is generally necessary for a definitive diagnosis. Elevated serum IgG4 concentrations are often but not always present.5Cardiovascular involvement may present as pseudotumors, periaortitis, coronary arteritis, and pericarditis.6Myocardial involvement is rare with only a handful of case reports documented in the literature. Although randomized data in this area are lacking, treatment is usually with immunosuppressive therapy. Most patients with IgG4-RD will respond rapidly to corticosteroids, which are considered first-line treatment; however, steroid-sparing agents can also be used. For recurrent or refractory cases, B-cell depletion with rituximab appears to be a useful approach. In select cases, surgical resection with adjuvant immunotherapy can also be considered.1,2,7 This case illustrates the effect of rituximab on a large intracardiac mass secondary to IgG4-RD that was deemed inoperable and refractory to conventional steroid treatment. The case also posed a diagnostic challenge given the history of Burkitt lymphoma and highlights the importance of careful clinical correlation, multimodality imaging, and histopathological analysis in the diagnosis of IgG4-related disease. The patient was asymptomatic at 10 months after completion of rituximab immunotherapy, and cardiac imaging showed no evidence of progressive disease.

scenario: A man in his early 70s with a history of permanent atrial fibrillation treated with atrioventricular junction ablation and biventricular pacemaker implantation was hospitalized with decompensated heart failure and acute kidney injury. His history was notable for nonischemic cardiomyopathy with ejection fraction of 40% and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, for which he underwent single-lung transplant 9 years prior. Following diuresis and medical optimization, repeated echocardiogram showed a newly depressed ejection fraction (30%). His electrocardiogram (ECG) was notable for alternating QRS morphologies (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) pacing vector was programmed from LV tip to right ventricular (RV) lead ring. During pacemaker threshold testing, a change in QRS morphology was observed as the output was reduced (Figure 1B). Chest radiography revealed severe right pulmonary fibrosis leading to ipsilateral mediastinal shift and pacemaker lead position unchanged from implantation.
explanation: C. Change the LV pacing configuration The diagnosis of anodal capture is strongly suggested by the sudden change in QRS configuration during the LV threshold test (Figure 1B). Further, LV pacing should produce a right bundle branch block morphology (predominantly positive QRS in V1), which is not observed and raises the possibility of anodal capture. In the above LV threshold test, the paced vector (from LV lead to RV lead) resulted in concurrent capture of both the LV and RV tissue at high output. At diminishing output, left ventricular capture was lost while RV capture (anodal capture) persisted. This RV capture QRS morphology was identical to the QRS morphology when pacing from the RV lead. This is consistent with anodal stimulation, defined as pure or predominant RV capture when LV pacing. Cardiac electrical dyssynchrony is a cause of mechanical inefficiency and worsening heart failure. Placement of RV and LV leads allows for electrical resynchronization with a biventricular pacemaker. LV leads can pace in multiple configurations to avoid phrenic nerve capture or areas of scar. One common pacing configuration is to drive electrical current from the LV lead (cathode) to the RV lead (anode). When the LV tissue is diseased and difficult to excite electrically, this pacing configuration is susceptible to RV myocardial capture without LV myocardial excitation,1,2a phenomenon originally termedanodal capture.3 Identification of anodal capture requires close examination of the surface ECG by the treating physician. A biventricular pacemaker is unable to detect this phenomenon and will give a false sense of reassurance that resynchronization is occurring. In this patient’s case, device interrogation suggested that effective biventricular pacing was occurring 98% of the time while the surface ECG demonstrated that this number was closer to 66%. Previous studies have demonstrated that unrecognized anodal capture can account for failure to respond to resynchronization therapy.4,5The preferred treatment for this problem is to adjust the pacing configuration to exclude the RV lead. Of note, while this patient had a bipolar LV lead, more modern quadripolar LV leads allow multiple LV-only pacing configurations that prevent anodal capture by obviating LV to RV pacing. Finally, anodal capture is seen almost exclusively in pacemakers as the large defibrillation coil in implantable cardioverter-defibrillator leads requires much higher current to excite the RV myocardium.6 For this patient, the LV pacing configuration was changed to a true bipolar LV configuration (LV distal to proximal electrode) and a pure LV capture morphology was observed (Figure 2). Unfortunately, the patient died of complications from recurrent diverticulitis with perforation, precluding repeated echocardiographic assessment of his cardiomyopathy following adjustment of his pacing configuration.

An electrocardiogram (ECG;Figure 1A) showed diffuse ST-segment elevation, most prominently in the anterior precordial leads. explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy complicated by hypotension secondary to LV outflow tract obstruction and LV thrombus Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC), also calledstress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by transient, reversible, regional systolic and diastolic dysfunction, usually involving the LV apex and midventricle, with hyperkinesia of the basal LV segments.1Unfortunately, the patient also developed LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and hemodynamic instability. This is more frequent in elderly patients with TTC and is associated with septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet.2It was confirmed by cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), which demonstrated an interventricular septal thickness greater than or equal to 12 mm and a systolic jet in the LVOT because of dynamic obstruction (Video). The prevalence of LVOT obstruction in TTC ranges from 19% to 25%, whereas 10% to 20% of patients with TTC develop cardiogenic shock.3Thus, in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation complicated by hypotension, swift recognition of TTC is clinically imperative because of its unique clinical management requirements. Inotropic agents and intra-aortic balloon pumps used for the treatment of cardiogenic shock attributable to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) can exacerbate shock and catastrophic sequelae in patients with TTC and LVOT obstruction. In a registry study of 541 patients with TTC,4LV thrombi were relatively infrequent but more likely in women with apical ballooning and increased cardiac troponin levels, which was consistent with this case. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing several features of diffuse ST-segment elevation, shock secondary to LVOT obstruction, and LV thrombus with acute TTC. An ECG is an initial screening test in patients with suspected TTC or STEMI. Studies have reported that ST-segment elevation in TTC occurs diffusely and most commonly in the anterior precordial leads, while ST depression (ie, reciprocal change) is a less common finding, which represents a possibility to establish a differential diagnosis based on ECG criteria. However, the criteria differentiating TTC from STEMI because of wraparound left anterior descending artery occlusion can often be challenging. The International Takotsubo Registry study has demonstrated that ST-segment depression in aVR provides a high specificity and positive predictive value for detecting TTC when associated with ST elevation in the anteroseptal leads.5Also, ECG patterns of patients with TTC are diverse, and the prevalence of T-wave inversion in the setting of ST-elevation is higher than that of patients with STEMI. Also, there is a trend toward longer QTc intervals on admission ECG in TTC. Importantly, in the diffuse ST-elevation setting, concomitant ST depression in aVR, T-wave inversion, and prolongation of the QTc interval may be clinically important to differentiate TTC from STEMI. Any unexplainable cardiac abnormalities with hemodynamic instability should alert the clinician to the possibility of TTC and necessity of separate treatment approaches for managing cardiogenic shock. The patient received urgent fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution at 5 to 10 mL/kg/h over the first 2 hours (total volume, 2000 mL) and β-blocker therapy with bisoprolol at 2.5 mg per day, which gradually improved her hemodynamics. Anticoagulant therapy was also initiated for the LV thrombus. Myocardial T2 mapping revealed a higher T2 value in the midapical lesion, corresponding to the extent of apical ballooning, without myocardial scarring on late gadolinium-enhanced CMR (Figure 2). The apical ballooning returned to normal in a few months, accompanied with a dramatic improvement of myocardial tissue abnormalities and the disappearance of the thrombus and LVOT obstruction, thus confirming the initial diagnosis of TTC.

scenario: A woman in her 70s was referred to our centralized heart failure management program because of New York Heart Association functional class III heart failure with preserved left ventricular systolic function and recurrent hospitalizations for heart failure. Her medical history was remarkable for coronary artery disease after coronary artery bypass grafting, chronic stable angina, severe tricuspid regurgitation, atrial fibrillation, and obesity with a body mass index of 39 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared). After screening and medication optimization, she underwent successful implantation of a small sensor-pressure device (CardioMEMS; Abbott) into her pulmonary artery without complication. Her home medications included torsemide, metolazone, metoprolol succinate, spironolactone, isosorbide mononitrate, diltiazem, and ranolazine. Her initial postimplantation sensor readings and waveforms are shown inFigure 1A. The patient transmitted readings daily without event, and her medications were adjusted to target a pulmonary artery diastolic pressure less than 20 mm Hg. A week and a half after implant, sensor readings were difficult to obtain. After asking the patient to transmit readings while on her stomach rather than supine, pressure readings were able to be obtained (Figure 1B).

Obtain a chest radiograph In managing patients with implanted CardioMEMS sensors, it is not unusual to have to troubleshoot pulmonary artery pressure readings, connectivity challenges, or abnormal readings suggestive of electromechanical interference. This case presented a different challenge in that after positional adjustment a tracing was recorded, but the waveform recorded in the prone position showed loss of the dicrotic notch, suggesting late device migration to the right ventricle, as confirmed on chest radiography (Figure 2). The CardioMEMS heart failure system allows for ambulatory heart failure management by targeting pulmonary artery pressures to maintain euvolemia. The device is approved for use in patients with New York Heart Association class III heart failure who have been previously hospitalized for heart failure.1The device is implanted percutaneously in a segmental pulmonary artery, calibrated in real time with a pulmonary artery catheter, and interrogated remotely at home using an electromagnetic receiver that transmits centrally to a cloud storage platform. Meticulous attention to vessel sizing and device placement is required to ensure that the distal nitinol loop is adequately secured within a segmental pulmonary artery, but not too deep so that the sensor itself becomes overendothelialized, which can lead to late signal loss or signal dampening. When readings cannot be obtained, troubleshooting commonly involves switching the receiver’s connection to Wi-Fi or cellular, repositioning of the receiver pillow, and adjusting the environment to reduce electromechanical interference (eg, from heating blankets). Differential diagnosis includes sensor malfunction requiring recalibration with right heart catheterization or the rare event of device migration, which can be confirmed with chest radiography. Query of the MAUDE database, a passive surveillance system through the US Food and Drug Administration that collects voluntary reports of device-related adverse events, found that among 5500 implants, sensor failure, malfunction, or migration occurred in 46 cases. Of these, 35 required recalibration, 13 reimplantation, and 11 hospitalization (for reintervention, heart failure, or overdiuresis). Five sensors could not be used despite recalibration.2Sensor migration is most likely to happen during the implant procedure itself; however, late implant migration has been rarely described.3Rali and colleagues3reported late migration of a CardioMEMS sensor from the left pulmonary artery to the right lung approximately 4 months after placement. A chest radiograph was obtained (Figure 2), which visualized the sensor in the right ventricle. This position was confirmed with transesophageal echocardiography that was performed as part of an ongoing evaluation for severe tricuspid regurgitation, which showed prominent tethering of the tricuspid valve leaflets with the displaced CardioMEMS device lodged in the subvalvular apparatus (Video). Live fluoroscopy confirmed that the device was not mobile and, as such, no intervention was performed. Pressure tracings are now obtained daily with the patient lying on her stomach and used to manage her heart failure to maintain euvolemia.

scenario: A man in his mid-50s with a medical history significant for pulmonary embolism 10 years prior (previously receiving anticoagulation therapy) presented to the emergency department with 10 days of progressively worsening, sharp, nonradiating chest pain. The pain was present at rest, 7 of 10 in severity, and worse with inspiration. He experienced concomitant exertional shortness of breath, dry cough, and lightheadedness. His cardiac history was otherwise unremarkable. Family history was notable for breast cancer in his mother and his sister, but no known inherited hypercoagulable disorders. In the emergency department, his vital signs were as follows: temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 130/76 mm Hg, heart rate 97/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. Physical examination results were unremarkable, with no cardiac murmurs, rubs, pulmonary crackles, jugular venous distention, or lower extremity edema. Laboratory test results were remarkable for an elevated D-dimer level, an elevated C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a mildly elevated pro-BNP level, but normal levels of troponin and procalcitonin. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with evidence of right heart strain, and a computed tomography angiogram of the chest demonstrated an occlusive pulmonary embolism of the left main pulmonary artery and several peripheral consolidations in the left lower lung field consistent with infarction. The patient started anticoagulation therapy with intravenous heparin. A subsequent echocardiogram revealed bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle and a very large (6.6 × 4.1-cm), mobile, nonhomogeneous, pedunculated mass straddling the tricuspid valve and moving between the right atrium and right ventricle (Figure 1andVideo).

explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.

explanation: D.Begin the process of periodic cardiac screening with speckle-tracking echocardiography and radionuclide cardiac scintigraphy. Patients may receive genetic testing, via saliva or blood, for known or likely pathogenicTTRvariants through a variety of approaches as follows: (1) clinical testing ordered by a physician, (2) direct-to-consumer testing initiated by the patient, and (3) research testing as part of a study. Clinical testing companies are required by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to maintain Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments certification and typically report all pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified in theTTRgene. There are more than 100 pathogenic mutations in theTTRgene with considerable phenotypic heterogeneity, ranging from predominantly neurologic to cardiac phenotypes. Hereditary transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (hATTR-CA) is an autosomal dominant disease with variable penetrance for which targeted therapy is now available. The substitution of valine for isoleucine at position 122 (Val122Ile, SNPrs76992529) and threonine for alanine at position 60 (Thr60Ala, SNPrs121918070) are the 2 most common variants leading to hATTR-CA in the US.1,2 Similar to rare variants in other cardiomyopathy genes, the genotype-phenotype associations for other rare variants inTTRare not as well studied given their low frequency. Thus, the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics has created a scoring system for interpreting genetic variants using population databases, computational predictive algorithms, functional data, and segregation analysis (Table).3The ClinGen database provides expert curation and variant classification. The variant identified in this patient (Ser97Tyr) is rare, is located in a mutational hot spot, and has a deleterious effect on the protein function based on computational analyses.4Multiple case series document that onset of disease for Ser97Tyr variant ranges from 46 to 70 years of age. While initial presentation was sensorimotor polyneuropathy, as in this patient, a majority had evidence of hATTR-CA on additional workup, and multiple patients experienced sudden cardiac death. Given the totality of these findings, this variant is interpreted as pathogenic. Although echocardiography and cardiac scintigraphy are established imaging modalities to support a clinical diagnosis of hATTR-CA, data for screening in asymptomatic carriers of pathogenic variants are limited. There is some evidence in favor of screening with cardiac scintigraphy. In small studies of asymptomatic carriers of a pathogenicTTRvariant, those with radiotracer uptake on cardiac scintigraphy developed symptomatic heart failure within 5 years.5,6Data from the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults study demonstrated that Black adults with the Val122Ile variant had impaired left ventricular circumferential strain.7While the differences in strain were small, the ease of use and low risk profile make speckle-tracking echocardiography (STE) a viable screening tool. The 2019 expert recommendations rated echocardiography and radionuclide scintigraphy as “appropriate” in asymptomatic carriers of a pathogenicTTRvariant.8Initiation of screening is recommended 10 years before the typical age at onset and repeated every 3 to 5 years.9While these clinical recommendations can be useful, they are based on limited available evidence. Given that individuals with the Ser97Tyr variant can present as early as the fifth decade of life, screening this patient now with STE and cardiac scintigraphy is a reasonable next step. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is an alternative imaging modality to detect early signs of hATTR-CA. Late gadolinium enhancement, elevated native T1, and high extracellular volume fraction may help identify disease earlier in asymptomatic carriers.10Use of cardiac magnetic resonance imaging in asymptomatic carriers was rated as “may be appropriate” by the expert recommendations.8 The patient underwent STE and cardiac scintigraphy. Neither test identified any abnormalities. The patient was recommended to undergo routine surveillance testing every 3 to 5 years or with development of any cardiovascular symptoms. All first-degree relatives were recommended to undergo cascade testing and consider further screening for hATTR-CA.

explanation: Kounis syndrome (acute coronary vasospasm associated with anaphylactoid response) C. Give a second dose of 0.5 mg of intramuscular epinephrine Kounis syndrome is a pathological state of acute coronary vasospasm with mast cell degranulation and interaction with other inflammatory cells secondary to allergic or hypersensitivity and anaphylactic or anaphylactoid insults.1,2The inflammatory mediators involved include histamine, arachidonic acid, neutral protease, and platelet-activating factors.1,3Coronary arteries can be the primary site during anaphylaxis and result in Kounis syndrome manifestations.1,3Kounis syndrome can be precipitated by many factors, including angioedema, urticaria, hay fever, food allergy,Hymenopterastings, latex, and drugs.1,2 Three variants of Kounis syndrome have been described. Type 1 includes patients with normal or near-normal coronary arteries without predisposing factors for coronary artery disease, in whom the acute release of inflammatory mediators induce coronary artery spasm attributable to endothelial dysfunction with or without an increase of cardiac enzymes and troponins.1Type 2 includes quiescent preexisting atheromatous disease, in whom acute release of inflammatory mediators induce coronary artery spasm with plaque erosion or rupture, manifesting as acute myocardial infarction.1,4Type 3 includes patients with coronary artery stent thrombosis.4 A high index of suspicion is of paramount importance, since the diagnosis might be easily overlooked.5In the settings of allergic reactions, the presence of a cardiac symptom profile, such as acute chest pain, chest discomfort, dyspnea, palpitations, tachycardia or bradycardia, hypotension, cold extremities, diaphoresis, or cardiac arrest, must raise the suspicion for Kounis syndrome.1 The ECG may show a variety of abnormalities, including ST-segment depression or elevation, atrial fibrillation, sinus bradycardia or tachycardia, T-wave flattening or inversion, atrioventricular block, bigeminal rhythm, ventricular ectopic beats, and ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.1Serum levels of tryptase are elevated during an episode.3However, cardiac injury biomarkers, such as cardiac enzymes and troponins, may or may not be elevated.3 The management of Kounis syndrome includes treatment of both anaphylactic shock (initially with intramuscular epinephrine) and acute coronary syndrome.4Type 1 is managed with intravenous corticosteroids, H1 and H2 antihistamines, and analgesia. Type 2 is managed as per the acute coronary event protocol, along with corticosteroids and antihistamines. Type 3 requires urgent harvest of the intrastent thrombus along with corticosteroids and antihistamines. The use of additional drugs must be done cautiously, because nitroglycerine causes hypotension, β-blockers can cause coronary artery spasm, and morphine might result in mast cell degranulation.5After the resolution of the acute event, a full cardiology workup, including 12-lead ECG, echocardiogram, and evaluation for modifiable cardiac risk factors, must be performed, along with follow-up with an allergy or immunology specialist.3 The patient’s presentation was consistent with anaphylaxis and possibly cold-induced urticaria. In the emergency department, they were treated with intramuscular epinephrine, methylprednisolone, ondansetron, diphenhydramine, and famotidine, with improvement. After the resolution of symptoms, a repeated ECG showed resolution of a multilead ST-segment depression (Figure 2). The patient had normal biochemistry test results, except for an elevated high-sensitivity troponin I level of 486.0 ng/L (normal range, ≤26 ng/L; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1.0), which normalized within 16 hours during admission. The presentation was consistent with Kounis syndrome or anaphylactic coronary artery vasospasm, given the presence of anaphylaxis and ECG changes. They had an uncomplicated short admission to the internal medicine service. After consultation with the cardiology service, it was decided not to pursue coronary angiography, since symptoms had resolved and ECG and troponin results had normalized. On discharge, they were referred to an allergist and a medical genetics consultant, with instructions to carry an EpiPen always.

explanation: Right coronary artery compression by the right ventricular angulation of the RVS-ECMO cannula C. Reposition the cannula and repeat the angiogram The key to the diagnosis is recognizing the potential of cannulae within the right ventricle to compress the RCA (Figure 2;Video 2). While this may not be clinically significant, as in the present case, it may result in malignant arrhythmias or myocardial infarction. Failure to recognize and correct this phenomenon may lead to unnecessary procedures, such as a coronary intervention. Since patient mobilization prior to lung transplant improves posttransplant outcomes, dual-lumen cannulae, such as ProtekDuo, placed from the right internal jugular vein are increasingly used for VV ECMO1-3to promote preoperative and postoperative mobilization of patients receiving lung transplants. The most common complications of VV ECMO include vascular injury, bleeding, and hemolysis,2,4but myocardial infarction secondary to coronary artery compression has been described.5This report illustrates how the hinge point of the RVS-ECMO cannula in the right ventricle of the RCA may cause extrinsic compression to the RCA. A U-shaped configuration of the cannula, with a less acute angle, is less likely to cause this than a more acute V-shape configuration. If a V shape is recognized after advancing the distal tip of the cannula to the desired position, we advise retracting the cannula under fluoroscopic guidance, which attenuates the angle at the hinge point of the cannula. The RVS-ECMO cannula was repositioned at the time of catheterization. The patient remained hemodynamically stable without cardiac complaints. He subsequently underwent a successful lung transplant.

scenario: A middle-aged woman presented with chest pain, elevated troponin-T of 1037 ng/L (normal <14 ng/L; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1), and anterior T-wave inversion on electrocardiography. She was a smoker with hypertension and kidney dysfunction, with a history of left-sided paresthesia. Coronary angiography demonstrated unobstructed coronary arteries. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging revealed subendocardial midinferolateral late gadolinium enhancement with corresponding hypokinesis consistent with a partial-thickness myocardial infarction. Prolonged Holter monitoring showed no evidence of atrial fibrillation. Two years later, she had a similar presentation consistent with a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Repeated coronary angiography again demonstrated unobstructed coronary arteries. The CMR revealed the same midinferolateral late gadolinium enhancement as at the initial examination (Figure, A) but with focal enhancement on T2 short tau inversion recovery sequences (Figure, B), with increased T1 and T2 values suggestive of associated edema from an acute infarction in the same territory. A mobile interatrial septum was noted on 4-chamber cine imaging. A transthoracic echocardiogram bubble study demonstrated color flow at rest across the interatrial septum and a large shunt on Valsalva maneuver consistent with a grade 3 patent foramen ovale (PFO) (Video). Coincidentally, a brain MR scan to investigate the recurrent paresthesia revealed bilateral white matter lesions thought to be secondary to small-vessel disease greater in number than expected for the patient’s age, raising suspicion for microemboli.

explanation: Paradoxical embolism through PFO causing recurrent systemic embolism D. Closure of PFO and antiplatelet therapy A PFO is present in about 25% of the population and may coexist without etiologic implications in a patient with unexplained systemic embolism.1Owing to the complexity of variables involved and the lack of rigorous scientific evidence, no position can be made regarding quantitative assessment of the role of a PFO. Therefore, this should be evaluated with critical clinical judgment in an multidisciplinary setting, weighing up the following features on an individual basis: patient characteristics, imaging stroke/infarction pattern, PFO characteristics, and case-specific clinical clues.1An atrial septal aneurysm and/or a moderate to severe shunt are strongly associated with a causal role of PFO in patients with cryptogenic stroke in observational and randomized studies.2-6 Patent foramen ovale has been associated with systemic embolism to several organs.7A cryptogenic embolic event is defined as any definite ischemia occurring in an arterial bed without a known cause despite investigation.1Patients presenting with this picture should be screened for the presence of a PFO. When a PFO is thought likely to be implicated in a presumed cryptogenic embolic event, the event should then be classified as PFO-related instead of cryptogenic.8 Randomized clinical trials have shown superiority of PFO closure in reducing risk of recurrent ischemic stroke in certain patient subsets when compared with optimal medical therapy.9For patients who are open to all options, the BMJ Rapid Recommendations panel10make a weak recommendation for PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy rather than anticoagulant therapy. In all clinical scenarios, the 2 main tenets guiding treatment of PFO are the assessments of the probability that the PFO has a relevant role in the observed clinical picture and the likelihood that the observed clinical event will recur.1For patients with the highest probability of both, closure of the PFO should be advocated. For patients with the lowest probability, medical therapy should be considered.1For patients with intermediate probabilities, clinical judgment and discussion with the patient are required in appropriate decision-making.1 The position of the European Society of Cardiology is to perform percutaneous closure of a PFO in carefully selected patients between ages 18 to 65 years with a confirmed cryptogenic stroke, transient ischemic attack, or systemic embolism and an estimated high probability of a causal role of the PFO as assessed by clinical, anatomical, and imaging features.1 In deciding on postprocedural therapy, one should consider the following factors: (1) endothelialization of the device can continue up to 5 years following implantation; (2) device thrombosis is one of the most frequent complications following implantation; and (3) premature discontinuation of therapy may be associated with minor cerebrovascular events after PFO closure.1It is reasonable to propose dual antiplatelet therapy for 1 to 6 months after PFO closure.1Therapy with a single antiplatelet agent should be continued for at least 5 years.1The extension of therapy with a single antiplatelet beyond 5 years should be based on the balance between patient’s overall risk of stroke from other causes and bleeding risk.1 As in the case of this patient, paradoxical embolism across a large PFO should be considered in cases of myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries. Patent foramen ovale closure plus 1 to 6 months of dual antiplatelet therapy postprocedure was felt to be the treatment of choice owing to an estimated high probability of a causal role of the PFO with demonstrated recurrence in systemic embolism.

explanation: Spontaneous abnormal automaticity from a left lateral accessory pathway C. Electrophysiology study with or without catheter ablation The first ECG (Figure 1A) shows a wide QRS complex rhythm without visible atrial activity preceding ventricles. Right bundle branch block QRS morphology, positive concordance, and QRS axis (negative in leads I and aVL) support an activation arising from the laterobasal left ventricle. The second ECG (Figure 1B) shows sinus rhythm with a short PR interval and δ waves distinctive of ventricular preexcitation with an QRS axis compatible with an anterograde left lateral accessory pathway. These findings suggest that this wide QRS complex rhythm results from an abnormal automaticity from a left lateral accessory pathway. An electrophysiology study was performed after written informed consent. Electrophysiologic maneuvers confirmed the presence of a left lateral accessory pathway, and pacing from the distal coronary sinus (close to accessory pathway insertion) reproduced symptoms associated with similar wide QRS complex (Figure 2). The initial negative component in lead I, absent during sinus rhythm or pacing from the right atrium, reflects atrial activation originating from the accessory pathway region. A focal atrial tachycardia emerging close to accessory pathway insertion was the other hypothesized diagnosis; however, no atrial tachycardia was inducible during the procedure including after isoproterenol infusion. Moreover, the patient remained free from symptoms, and no atrial tachycardia was documented during the follow-up after accessory pathway radiofrequency ablation. Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia is a frequent cause of palpitations in patients with accessory pathways. Neck palpitations (frog sign) and headaches result from retrograde atrial depolarization with atrial contraction against closed atrioventricular valves during atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia episodes. Spontaneous automaticity has been reported in patients with atriofascicular accessory pathways (Mahaim fibers), with possible pacemaker-like cells in such accessory pathways with decremental properties,1,2and a few cases of automaticity or ventricular tachycardia originating from the ablation site have been reported after successful ablation of accessory pathways.3,4However, we report here a unique case of symptomatic spontaneous abnormal automaticity from an atrioventricular accessory pathway successfully managed by catheter ablation. Electrophysiology study indications have evolved and are now proposed systematically as a risk-stratifying tool in patients with pre-excitation (to assess accessory pathway refractory period) because (1) noninvasive markers such as intermittent pre-excitation during ambulatory monitoring or exercise testing have shown to be imperfect markers of a low-risk accessory pathway and (2) life-threatening arrhythmias have been reported even in asymptomatic patients.5Regarding other options, a pharmacologic approach with propafenone or flecainide is an alternative when ablation is not desirable or feasible. However, use of β-blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem or verapamil) must be restricted to patients without signs of pre-excitation on ECG because all medications that block the atrioventricular node may promote anterograde conduction through the accessory pathway in case of pre-excited atrial fibrillation.6-8
